newsitem.title: SWEDEN: AssiDoman threatens to pull out of Russia mill.
newsitem.headline: AssiDoman threatens to pull out of Russia mill.

text.p: Swedish forestry group AssiDoman said on Friday it would pull out of Russian paper and pulp mill Segezhabumprom unless a dispute over ownership was resolved.
The future of the mill remained uncertain after production stopped in March.
"From our side we have a long term interest in solving the remaining problems but not on just any terms," AssiDoman's managing director Lennart Ahlgren said in a statement.
"If we do not succeed in solving the ownership issue within the near future we will have to withdraw from our interest in Segezha."
AssiDoman, which is responsible for operations at the mill, said production was stopped due to the authorities delaying certain decisions, and a lack of oil and operating capital.
The major shareholders then decided not to give additional loans to the company until the debt situation and environmental and supply issues were solved.

AssiDoman said the economic, social and environmental issues had been to a great extent solved, but it was necessary to change the ownership structure at the mill to solve the financing of $100 million planned investments.
Stratton Paper Co, that holds 57 percent of the mill, is jointly owned by AssiDoman and Cyprus-based investment group Daventree.
The rest is owned by various groups with the Karelian state owning 20 percent and Russian timber and pulp sales company Upak 10 percent.
Stratton took over full operational and managerial control of the mill in January this year.
But Daventree has now said it is not prepared to participate with capital needed to restart the mill.
"Negotiations on the acquisition of Daventree's shares have not produced results," AssiDoman said in a statement.
AssiDoman said not all the necessary requirements to restart the mill were in place.
"We do not think it is reasonable that AssiDoman alone should contribute with equity and loans to Segezhabumprom for the benefit of the other shareholders," AssiDoman said.
